variables.title: Variables
variables.code:
let x = 10

(* Mutable reference *)
let y = ref 20
y := !y + 5
variables.notes: Variables are immutable by default. OCaml supports mutability via 'ref' for explicit references, which must be dereferenced with '!'.

data_types.title: Data Types
data_types.code:
let i : int = 42
let f : float = 3.14
let b : bool = true
let c : char = 'X'
let s : string = "Hello"

(* Variant type (ADT) *)
type shape = 
  | Circle of float
  | Rectangle of float * float
data_types.notes: OCaml has strong static typing with powerful inference. You rarely need to write type annotations.

operators.title: Operators
operators.code:
let add_int = 5 + 3
let add_float = 5.0 +. 3.0

let div_int = 5 / 2
let div_float = 5.0 /. 2.0

let logic = true && not false || true

let eq = 5 = 5
let phys_eq = 5 == 5
let neq = 5 <> 3
operators.notes: OCaml strictly separates integer and floating-point operators (e.g., '+' for int, '+.' for float). '=' is structural equality, '==' is physical equality.

conditionals.title: Conditionals
conditionals.code:
let result = 
  if x > 0 then
    "Positive"
  else
    "Non-positive"

(* Pattern matching as conditional *)
let sign = match x with
  | n when n > 0 -> 1
  | n when n < 0 -> -1
  | _ -> 0
conditionals.notes: if-then-else is an expression. Both branches must have the same type. Pattern matching is extremely common and powerful.

for_loop.title: For Loop
for_loop.code:
for i = 1 to 5 do
  Printf.printf "%d\n" i
done

(* Downward loop *)
for i = 5 downto 1 do
  Printf.printf "%d\n" i
done
for_loop.notes: OCaml includes imperative 'for' loops, mainly used for iterating over arrays or side effects. For lists, use List.map or List.iter.

while_loop.title: While Loop
while_loop.code:
let counter = ref 0 in
while !counter < 5 do
  Printf.printf "%d\n" !counter;
  counter := !counter + 1
done
while_loop.notes: OCaml has imperative 'while' loops, which are useful when dealing with mutable state (like refs) or side effects.

functions.title: Functions
functions.notes: Functions are defined using 'let'. The 'rec' keyword is required for recursive functions. Functions are automatically curried.

arrays.title: Arrays and Lists
arrays.code:
(* List (immutable, linked) *)
let lst = [1; 2; 3; 4]
let new_lst = 0 :: lst

(* Array (mutable, fixed size) *)
let arr = [| 1; 2; 3; 4 |]
arr.(0) <- 99
arrays.notes: Lists are immutable and great for functional programming. Arrays are mutable and allow O(1) random access.

maps.title: Maps
maps.code:
module StringMap = Map.Make(String)

let m = StringMap.empty
let m1 = StringMap.add "apple" 1 m
let m2 = StringMap.add "banana" 2 m1

let val_opt = StringMap.find_opt "apple" m2
maps.notes: Maps are created using functors (`Map.Make`). They are immutable and based on balanced AVL trees.

error_handling.title: Error Handling
error_handling.notes: OCaml supports exceptions for control flow and errors, but using 'option' or 'result' types is preferred for type-safe error handling.

comments.title: Comments & Annotations
comments.code:
-- Single-line comment
{- Multi-line
   comment block -}
add :: Int -> Int -> Int
add a b = a + b
comments.notes: OCaml uses functional comment delimiters (-- in Haskell/ML, ; in Lisps, # or % in BEAM).

numbers.title: Numbers & Numerics
numbers.notes: OCaml supports exact rational fractions, arbitrary-precision integers, and IEEE floats natively.

booleans.title: Booleans & Logic
booleans.notes: OCaml treats booleans as first-class algebraic constructors (True/False, true/false, t/nil).

type_casting.title: Type Conversion
type_casting.notes: OCaml performs conversion via typeclass methods (fromIntegral, show, read) or explicit parse functions.

strings.title: Strings & Text
strings.notes: OCaml represents strings as linked lists of characters, UTF-8 binaries, or dedicated text buffers.

string_formatting.title: String Formatting
string_formatting.code:
import Text.Printf
msg = printf "User %s scored %d" "Alice" (95 :: Int)
string_formatting.notes: OCaml formats text through format strings, interpolation macros, or string concatenation.

pattern_matching.title: Pattern Matching
pattern_matching.notes: Pattern matching is a core feature in OCaml, destructuring algebraic variants, tuples, and lists directly.

range.title: Ranges & Sequences
range.notes: OCaml constructs ranges as lazy lists, infinite streams, or structured range enumerables.

iterators.title: Iterators & Comprehensions
iterators.code: for x <- 1..10, rem(x, 2) == 0, do: x * x
iterators.notes: OCaml achieves iterative processing through list comprehensions, map/filter transforms, and recursion.

oop_classes.title: Types & Abstractions (OOP Equivalent)
oop_classes.code:
defmodule Person do
  defstruct [:name, :age]
  def greet(%Person{name: name}), do: "Hello #{name}"
end
oop_classes.notes: OCaml emphasizes algebraic data types, protocols/typeclasses, and structs over traditional class hierarchies.

lists.title: Lists (Linked Lists)
lists.notes: Lists in OCaml are singly linked immutable sequences optimized for head/tail structural sharing.

tuples.title: Tuples & Records
tuples.notes: OCaml uses fixed-length heterogeneous tuples for bundling related data points and function return values.

sets.title: Sets
sets.notes: OCaml provides persistent immutable sets implemented via balanced binary trees (HAMT / AVL).

modules_import.title: Modules & Imports
modules_import.code:
defmodule MyModule do
  import Enum, only: [map: 2]
  alias MyProject.Helper
end
modules_import.notes: OCaml isolates scopes through modules and explicit import lists with aliasing and qualified names.
